Look for the math

Huntington-Hill's method has been used by the US Congress since 1941. Its rounding rule is subtly different from ordinary rounding.

The equal-proportions cutoff

With ordinary rounding, a quota between L and L+1 is rounded up past the midpoint L + 1/2. The method of equal proportions instead uses the geometric mean sqrt(L(L+1)) as the cutoff. Equivalently, each additional seat goes to the state with the largest population / sqrt(s(s+1)), where s is the number of seats it already has.

What the check found

The logic test examines nearly two thousand random countries. Every allocation fills the house, states with zero population get no seats, the seat-by-seat priorities match an independent transcription, and the results agree with the Huntington-Hill column of the combined apportionment calculator on this site.

Compare the "Cutoff" column with the midpoint between the whole numbers around each quota. Which states round differently?
